entries.label: Astranis complies with U.S. Government space technology export regulations, therefore will you state which of the following applies to you:
What is the most impressive thing you have ever accomplished?
entries.value: Co-founding Open Health Intelligence and shipping ClarityAtlas into a live pilot at Johns Hopkins with 30+ users. I built the iOS product end to end in Swift and SwiftUI with Supabase on the backend, and the hardest piece was estimating sleep without a wearable, using HealthKit and Core Motion signals like step count, gait speed, and movement patterns as proxies. What made it feel like more than a class project was everything around the code. We recruited real users, refined the product thesis repeatedly, got into the Pava Spark Accelerator and NSF I-Corps, and received a non-binding investment indication of roughly $75,000 for about 7-8% equity, which we chose not to pursue immediately because we wanted the right long-term partners. We also pitched President Ron Daniels, which started when my cofounders and I spotted him during Lighting of the Quads, walked to Garland Hall, and knocked on locked doors until someone let us make the case. That turned into a formal meeting months later with Data Science and AI Institute leadership. The lesson was that building the thing is only part of making it real.

entries.label: Please describe the most impressive and complex project you have worked on. This can be from previous internships, school projects, or personal projects you took part in. Tell us what the project was, the technologies you used, challenges you faced, what specific role you played in this project, and what made this project complex or special.
entries.value: The most complex system I have built is the machine-learning core of an anomaly-detection and alert-prioritization platform at Summer Atlantic Capital / SAC Nexus. I own major parts of the data and ML infrastructure: the repository and CI scaffold, the event-ingestion pipeline, a versioned FastAPI microservice, and the public detection API. On the modeling side I do temporal sequence modeling over event streams with RNN and Transformer-style approaches, anomaly scoring, and a learning-to-rank layer that decides which alerts a human should see first. I also built an LLM explanation layer using retrieval-augmented generation so that a score turns into something an analyst can act on. The hard part was not raw detection accuracy. An anomaly system that fires constantly creates a second problem instead of solving the first, so ranking, explanation quality, and known failure modes mattered more than a marginal metric gain. That pushed me toward treating evaluation as a first-class engineering problem, which also came out of earlier work at Intelehealth where I built an evaluation framework comparing LLM-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case standard using stratified sampling to surface systematic failures.
